about: Two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, who are gods too, see that Vucub Caquix's pride is evil, and decide to shoot him with the blowgun while he eats and so put an end to his wealth and his jewels. The macaw has two sons as proud as he is: Zipacna, who plays with the great mountains and made them in a single night, and Cabracan, who shakes them; the father boasts that he is the sun, Zipacna that he made the earth, Cabracan that he shakes the sky. The boys hide among the leaves of the nance tree where the macaw comes to feed every day, and a pellet from the blowgun strikes him in the jaw, so that he falls to the ground. But when the boy (here called Hunhunahpu) runs to seize him, the macaw catches his arm, tears it off at the shoulder and carries it home, holding his jaw. He tells his wife Chimalmat that two demons have shot him and loosened his teeth, and hangs the arm over the fire until they come for it. The boys then ask an old man and an old woman, Zaqui Nimac and Zaqui Nima Tziz, to take them along to the macaw as their orphaned grandsons and to say that they are healers who draw the worms out of teeth. The old couple agree.

sentences.t: Vae vxe vchacatahic vyicoxic chi puch vꜫih Vucub Caquix cumal e caib ꜭaholab, Hunahpu vbi hun, Xbalanque vbi vcab.
sentences.l: This its-root his-being-brought-low, his-being-ruined(?) and-also his-day Seven Macaw by-them they two boys, Hunahpu his-name one, Xbalanque his-name its-second.
sentences.i: Here is the beginning of the downfall and the ruin of Vucub Caquix and of his day, at the hands of two boys: one was named Hunahpu, the second Xbalanque.
sentences.n: A new account begins, the fall of Vucub Caquix announced at the end of the last part. Vae 'this, here (is)' and vxe 'its root, its beginning' open it, as Are v xe opens the book. vchacatahic 'his being brought low': v- 'his' + chacatah, the verb of xchacatahic in the last part, + -ic, which makes a verbal noun; the sense is inferred, as there. vyicoxic is not otherwise known; it is paired with vchacatahic, and 'ruin' follows Brasseur's French ('destruction'), which is inferred. chi puch vꜫih: ꜫih is both 'day' and 'sun', and the macaw claimed to be the sun; Brasseur takes vꜫih as 'his glory'. How chi joins it to the pair is not clear. In vꜫih the q-shaped letter is read ꜫ (Brasseur g). cumal 'by them', with e caib ꜭaholab 'two boys': e marks the plural, caib is 'two', and ꜭahol is a man's son and also a young man, with -ab for the plural; the g-shaped letter is read ꜭ here and in every ꜭaholab and vꜭahol of this part. Hunahpu vbi hun, Xbalanque vbi vcab 'Hunahpu the name of one, Xbalanque the name of the second': vcab 'its second', from cab 'two'. Hunahpu is also a day of the calendar (the first part's Hunahpu Vuch, Hunahpu Vtiu). Brasseur takes Xbalanque as x-, a diminutive, + balam 'jaguar'; the make-up of the name is uncertain. The toggle shows Xb'alanke.

sentences.t: Xavi e cabauil.
sentences.l: Also they gods.
sentences.i: They too were gods.
sentences.n: A sentence with no verb: e 'they' before a noun, e cabauil 'they (were) gods'. cabauil 'god', the old K'iche' word for a deity, used in the first part of the Heart of Sky. xavi 'just so, also'; Brasseur takes it as 'truly' ('truly they were gods'). Either way the boys are not ordinary people.

sentences.t: Rumal iꜩel xquilo ri nimarizai rib, xrah vban chuvach Vꜭux Cah, xꜭha cu ri ꜭaholab: “Mavi vꜩ ta chuxoc; mavi chi ꜭaze vinac varal chuvach vleu.
sentences.l: Because evil they-saw the making-great(?) himself, he-wanted its-doing before Heart of-Sky, said then the boys: “Not good (ta) let-it-be; not that live person here on-face-of earth.
sentences.i: Because they saw as evil the one who made himself great, and what he wanted to do before the Heart of Sky, the boys said: “It is not good that this should be; people will not live here on the face of the earth.
sentences.n: iꜩel 'evil, bad' (modern itzel); ꜩ is Ximénez's tz ligature, printed ꜩ throughout (iꜩel, vꜩ, quiꜩih and the rest). xquilo 'they saw (it)': x- (completed action) + qui- 'they' + il 'see' + -o, the ending of a transitive verb. ri nimarizai rib 'the one making himself great': nimarizah 'make great' with rib 'himself', the macaw's boast in the last part; the ending -ai is not clear (Brasseur nimarizay), and 'the one who' is inferred. xrah vban 'he wanted its doing': xrah 'he wanted', with the wanted act as a possessed noun, vban (ban 'do'). chuvach Vꜭux Cah 'before the Heart of Sky'. xꜭha 'said' (x- + ꜭha 'say'), singular, though the boys are its subject: the manuscript's gh is read ꜭh here and in every xꜭha, xeꜭha and quix ꜭha of this part. In the boys' words, mavi ... ta 'not', with ta after what is denied; vꜩ 'good'; chuxoc 'let it be'. chi ꜭaze 'that (they) live': ꜭaze 'live, be alive', the root of ꜭazlem 'life'. With mavi it is taken as 'people will not (be able to) live'; Brasseur takes it as 'man not yet living here on the earth', and the sense is uncertain. In Vꜭux and ꜭaze the letter is q-shaped, not the g-shaped cuatrillo, and ꜭ was taken from Brasseur's reading (his q, qaze).

sentences.t: Quehe cut chi ca tih vvbaxic chuvi recha, chi ca vubah vi chiri, chi ca coh vi vyab, ta quizoc vꜫinomal, vxit, vpuvac, vcual, vyamanic ri cu cacabeh.
sentences.l: Thus then let we-try his-being-blowgunned on-top-of his-food, let we-blowgun(-him) there there, let we-put there his-sickness, then let-it-end(?) his-wealth, his-jade, his-silver, his-precious-stones(?), his-jewels(?) that he-cacabeh(?).
sentences.i: So let us try to shoot him with the blowgun at his food: let us shoot him there, let us put a sickness on him; and so let there be an end of his wealth, his jade, his silver, his precious stones, his jewels, the things he glories in.
sentences.n: chi ca 'let us': chi of wishing + ca- 'we', three times over, a triplet. tih 'try', as in the last part; here the ß-ligature is read ti (the manuscript has chicaßh). vvbaxic 'his being shot with the blowgun': v- 'his' + vb 'blowgun' (the hunting tube through which a clay pellet is blown) + -ax- (passive) + -ic. vubah 'shoot with the blowgun', a verb made from vb with -ah. recha 'his food': r- 'his' before a vowel + echa 'food'; the macaw's food is named below. coh 'put, place'; vyab 'his sickness' (yab 'sick'). ta quizoc is taken as ta 'so that' + quiz 'end, be finished' + -oc, the ending of chuxoc (Brasseur qiz-oc, his q = ꜭ; the toggle shows k'isoq, from the certain verb k'is 'end'). Five possessions follow, each with v- 'his': vꜫinomal 'his wealth' (modern q'inomal; the q-shaped letter read ꜫ, Brasseur g), vxit 'his jade', vpuvac 'his silver', and vcual, vyamanic, taken as 'precious stones' and 'jewels', as raxa cuval and yamanic in the macaw's boast in the last part; their exact senses are inferred. vcual is that cuval written without its v (Brasseur qual), and the toggle shows ukuwal, the kuwal of the last part. ri cu cacabeh: the manuscript runs cuca-|cabeh across a line, and Brasseur prints one word, gagabeh. It is divided here as cu + cacabeh, cu being c- (ongoing) + v- 'he', as in cu nimarizah 'he makes himself great'. The meaning of cacabeh is uncertain; 'the things he glories in' follows Brasseur ('dont il s'enorgueillit') and is a guess.

sentences.t: Quehe cut chubano ronohel vinac.
sentences.l: Thus then let-him-do(-it) all person.
sentences.i: For so all people would do.
sentences.n: chubano: ch- (a wish, or what is to come) + v- 'he', written u after ch, + bano 'do (it)'. ronohel vinac 'all people' takes the singular, as one body. The sense is inferred: if the macaw goes unchecked, everyone will do as he does (Brasseur 'so will everyone do').

sentences.t: Mavi are chi vinaquir vi ꜫaꜫal ri xa puvac.
sentences.l: Not this that come-into-being there glory the only silver.
sentences.i: Glory is not to come into being from what is only silver.
sentences.n: ꜫaꜫal 'glory, majesty' (modern q'aq'al), with the tresillo twice; it has the letters of ꜫaꜫ 'fire' with -al, but the link is not certain. vinaquir 'come into being', as in the first part. mavi are chi 'it is not that ... should'. ri xa puvac 'what is only silver': puvac is silver and any precious metal, the stuff of the macaw's boast. The line is taken as the boys' judgment that glory does not come from riches; Brasseur reads 'riches do not exist to swell his glory'. Both are inferred.

sentences.t: Ta chuxoc,” xeꜭha ri ꜭaholab, huhun chi vb qui telen, qui cabichal.
sentences.l: Then let-it-be,” they-said the boys, each with blowgun their telen(?), their cabichal(?).
sentences.i: So be it,” said the boys, each of them with a blowgun carried on the shoulder.
sentences.n: Ta chuxoc 'so be it', the creators' word of assent in the first part, now the boys'. xeꜭha 'they said', plural. huhun 'each one' (hun 'one' doubled). chi vb 'with a blowgun' (modern ub'). qui telen, qui cabichal is a couplet whose words are not otherwise known; telen may belong with vteleb 'his shoulder' below, and Brasseur's French has 'each with his blowgun on his shoulder'. i follows him and gives the pair as one phrase; the sense is inferred.

sentences.t: Are cu ri Vucub Caquix e caib vꜭahol: are nabe al ri Zipacna; vcabal chi cut ri Cabracan; Chimalmat cut vbi qui chuch, rixoquil ri Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: This then the Seven Macaw they two his-sons: this first child the Zipacna; its-second in-turn then the Cabracan; Chimalmat then her-name their mother, his-wife the Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: Vucub Caquix had two sons: the first-born was Zipacna, and the second was Cabracan; and Chimalmat was the name of their mother, the wife of Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: e caib vꜭahol 'two (were) his sons', with no verb, as e cabauil above. nabe al 'the first child': al is a mother's child, as in Alom. vcabal 'the second': cab 'two' with v- and -al. In vcabal the c is retraced in heavy ink and looks like a k, a letter Ximénez does not use elsewhere; it is printed c (Brasseur u cabal). chi cut is taken as chic 'in turn' with its c shared with cut, as in the earlier parts. rixoquil 'his wife': r- + ixoc 'woman' + -il. The names: Zipacna, written Zipaçna with a cedilla at this first occurrence and with plain c after it (printed c throughout; Brasseur finds no clear sense in it); Cabracan, which Brasseur says Ximénez renders 'of two legs' (cab 'two' + racan 'his leg', compare Huracan) and which he himself takes for the earthquake, both uncertain; Chimalmat, which Brasseur compares with Nahuatl chimalli 'shield', also uncertain. The toggle shows Kab'raqan, with the q of Huracan's Juraqan.

sentences.t: Are cu ri Zipacna are chire chaah ri nimac huiub, ri Chicac, Hunahpu, Pecul, Yaxcanul, Macamob, Huliznab, chuchaxic vbi huiub xꜭolic ta chi zaquiric;
sentences.l: This then the Zipacna this for-him playing(?) the great mountains, the Chicac, Hunahpu, Pecul, Yaxcanul, Macamob, Huliznab, it-is-said its-name mountains were-there when (chi) it-dawned;
sentences.i: As for Zipacna, his play was with the great mountains, Chicac, Hunahpu, Pecul, Yaxcanul, Macamob and Huliznab, as the mountains are called that were there when the dawn came;
sentences.n: chire chaah: the manuscript runs the words together (chirechaah), and they are divided as Brasseur divides them. chire 'to him, for him'; chaah is taken as 'play (at ball)', from Brasseur's note, which gives the phrase word for word as 'of him to play'; his French has Zipacna rolling the mountains about. The sense is inferred. ri nimac huiub 'the great mountains': nimac is nim 'great' with the plural -ac. The image clearly has nimac here, where Brasseur prints napak; the image is followed. huiub is huyub 'mountain' written with i for y (the next paragraph has both spellings); the toggle shows juyub'. Six mountains are named, and the names are kept; Ximénez writes plain c in Chicac and Yaxcanul. Brasseur places them in Guatemala, taking Hunahpu for the Volcán de Fuego above Antigua and Yaxcanul for the Santa María volcano near Quetzaltenango. chuchaxic 'as they are called' is the house word chuꜭhaxic, here written with plain ch; the toggle shows chuch'axik, as in the first part. xꜭolic 'they were there': x- + ꜭol 'be (in a place)' + -ic; the g-shaped letter is read ꜭ (Brasseur qolic). ta chi zaquiric 'when it dawned' (zac 'white').

sentences.t: xa hun aꜫab chi vinaquiric rumal ri Zipacna.
sentences.l: only one night in coming-into-being by the Zipacna.
sentences.i: in a single night they came into being through Zipacna.
sentences.n: xa hun aꜫab 'only one night' (aꜫab with the tresillo). chi vinaquiric 'in coming into being': vinaquir + -ic, the verbal noun. rumal 'by, through'. Brasseur reads it the same way: the mountains were made in one night by Zipacna's power.

sentences.t: Are ri chi cu ri Cabracan chi zilab huiub rumal, chi nebouic chuti huiub, nima huyub rumal.
sentences.l: This the in-turn then the Cabracan, that move(?) mountain by-him, that tremble(?) small mountain, great mountain by-him.
sentences.i: And Cabracan in his turn: by him the mountains were moved, by him the small mountains and the great mountains shook.
sentences.n: chi in Are ri chi cu is again taken as chic 'in turn'. Then two clauses with chi, 'that ... move, that ... tremble', each with rumal 'by him'. zilab 'move, stir' (compare xzilibatah 'was shaken loose' below) and nebouic 'tremble, sway' are inferred from Brasseur's French ('moved the mountains ... the mountains great and small shook'). chuti huiub, nima huyub 'small mountains, great mountains', a pair that means all the mountains. In chuti the ß-ligature is read ti (the manuscript has chußhuiub), and Ximénez writes huiub and huyub side by side; the toggle shows juyub' for both.

sentences.t: Xavi quehe nimarizabal quib xquibano vꜭahol Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: Just thus making-great themselves they-did his-sons Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: In the same way the sons of Vucub Caquix made themselves great.
sentences.n: nimarizabal 'a making great': nimarizah, the macaw's verb, with -abal, the ending of means and place, here with quib 'themselves' (qui- 'their' + ib 'self'). xquibano 'they did (it)': x- + qui- 'they' + ban 'do' + -o. vꜭahol 'his sons', with no plural ending.

sentences.t: “Ix va, in ꜫih,” xꜭha Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: “You this, I sun,” said Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: “Look, all of you: I am the sun,” said Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: The three boasts follow, one each. Ix 'you (pl.)', va 'this, here': Brasseur's note gives 'You! here am I the sun', as if he said 'you, look'. in ꜫih 'I (am the) sun', with no verb, as e cabauil 'they (were) gods'. In ꜫih the q-shaped letter is read ꜫ (Brasseur g). The macaw repeats the claim of the last part.

sentences.t: “In va, in banol vleu,” xꜭha ri Zipacna.
sentences.l: “I this, I maker earth,” said the Zipacna.
sentences.i: “Here am I: I am the maker of the earth,” said Zipacna.
sentences.n: banol 'maker': ban 'make, do' + -ol, the ending of agent nouns, as in Ꜯacol, Bitol. Zipacna, who made the mountains in a night, claims the earth.

sentences.t: “In chi cut quiyou cah, chin vlih ronohel vleu,” xꜭha ri Cabracan.
sentences.l: “I in-turn then I-shake(?) sky, I-shall-bring-down(?) all earth,” said the Cabracan.
sentences.i: “And I shake the sky, and I shall bring down the whole earth,” said Cabracan.
sentences.n: quiyou is taken as c- (ongoing) + in 'I', its n not written (as in quiꜭohe 'I am' in the last part), + you, a verb 'shake' (Brasseur 'I shake the sky'); the form and the sense are inferred. chin vlih 'I shall bring down': ch- (what is to come) + in 'I' + vlih, taken as the verb of vvlih 'fell in' in the last part, here with ronohel vleu 'all the earth' after it; inferred. Sky and earth, cah and vleu, the pair of the first part: Cabracan claims the whole world.

sentences.t: Xavi vꜭahol Vucub Caquix, xavi chi vi xquicam vi qui nimal chirih qui cahau.
sentences.l: Just his-sons Seven Macaw, just (chi) there they-took there their greatness behind their father.
sentences.i: So too the sons of Vucub Caquix: they too took their greatness after their father.
sentences.n: xavi ... xavi 'just so ... just so'. xquicam 'they took': x- + qui- 'they' + cam 'take', the verb of xchicacam 'we shall take' in the first part, not cam 'die'. Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q (that is ꜭ), and the toggle shows k'am. The chi of chi vi is not clear here; vi 'there' stands twice. qui nimal 'their greatness' (nim 'great' + -al). chirih qui cahau 'behind their father': chi + r- 'its' + ih 'back', so 'following their father'.

sentences.t: Are cut iꜩel xquil ri ꜭaholab; maha chi bantah oc ca nabe chuch, ca nabe cahau.
sentences.l: This then evil they-saw the boys; not-yet that be-made yet our first mother, our first father.
sentences.i: This was the evil the boys saw; and our first mother, our first father had not yet been made.
sentences.n: xquil 'they saw', the verb of xquilo above, here without the -o. maha ... oc 'not yet', as in the last part (maha oc ca zaquir oc). bantah 'be made, come to be done', from ban 'make, do' (compare xbanatahic). ca nabe chuch, ca nabe cahau 'our first mother, our first father', a couplet. 'our' is the narrator's, the K'iche' who tell the story, and the first parents are the people still to be made (Brasseur: the men the K'iche' held to be their ancestors).

sentences.t: Quehe cut xnohix vi qui camic, qui zachic cumal ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: Thus then was-conceived(?) there their death, their loss by-them boys.
sentences.i: And so their death, their undoing, was planned by the boys.
sentences.n: xnohix 'it was conceived, planned': x- + noh 'think out' + -ix, a passive; inferred, as in the third part (Brasseur here 'was resolved'). qui camic, qui zachic 'their death, their loss', a couplet of verbal nouns: cam 'die' and zach 'be lost' (as xoh zach in the last part), each + -ic. 'their' means the macaw and his sons. cumal 'by them', with ꜭaholab.

sentences.t: Vae cute vvbaxic Vucub Caquix cumal caib ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: This then his-being-blowgunned Seven Macaw by-them two boys.
sentences.i: Here, then, is how Vucub Caquix was shot with the blowgun by the two boys.
sentences.n: A large capital V begins the episode of the shooting, and so a new paragraph. cute, a longer form of cut 'then'. vvbaxic 'his being shot with the blowgun', as in the boys' plan: v- 'his' + vb 'blowgun' + -ax- + -ic. The toggle shows uub'axik: the possessive u- before ub'.

sentences.t: Xchicabyih qui chacatahic chi qui huhunal ri nimarizai rib.
sentences.l: We-shall-tell their being-brought-low of their each-one the making-great(?) himself.
sentences.i: We shall tell how they were brought low, each one of them who made himself great.
sentences.n: Xchicabyih 'we shall tell': xchi- 'shall' + ca- 'we' + byih 'say', the narrator's word at the end of the last part. The i after ch is a blot in the manuscript and is read as there. qui chacatahic 'their being brought low', the verbal noun of xchacatahic, with qui- 'their': the father and the two sons. chi qui huhunal 'each one of them': huhun 'each' + -al. ri nimarizai rib 'the one making himself great', as above, in the singular: each in turn.

sentences.t: Are ri Vucub Caquix hun nima che ri tapal; are cu recha ri Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: This the Seven Macaw one great tree the tapal; this then his-food the Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: Vucub Caquix had one great tree, a nance; it was the food of Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: Are ri Vucub Caquix 'as for Vucub Caquix': are sets the topic, and no verb follows. tapal is the nance, a tree of the warm lands with small, round, yellow, fragrant fruit; so Brasseur's note, which gives its Spanish name nanze. are cu recha 'it was his food': recha, r- 'his' + echa 'food', as in the boys' plan.

sentences.t: Are chulo ri vvach tapal, chacan chui che hutaꜫih;
sentences.l: This he-comes(?) the its-fruit tapal, climbs(?) on-top-of tree every-day;
sentences.i: he would come to the fruit of the nance and climb to the top of the tree every day;
sentences.n: chulo is taken from vl 'come here, arrive' with ch-; the form is not clear (Brasseur 'he came to the nance'). vvach tapal 'the fruit of the tapal': vach is 'face' and also 'fruit', the face a tree shows (compare vachinic in the last part). chacan is taken as ch- + acan 'climb', the verb of que rah acanic in the last part; Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur prints ch'akan, and the toggle gives the root as aq'an, as there. The same letters, in xe chacanic, were taken in the third part as one word, 'go on all fours' (toggle chakanik); here Brasseur's division ch'akan and the climb to the top of the tree decide, and the reading is inferred. chui che 'on top of the tree': chui is chuvi without its v (as ruma for rumal in the last part); the toggle respells the letters. hutaꜫih 'every day' (hun 'one' + tac 'each' + ꜫih 'day'), with the q-shaped letter read ꜫ (Brasseur g).

sentences.t: xilom acut rechabal cumal ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: had-been-seen(?) then his-feeding-place by-them the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: and the place where he fed had been seen by Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: xilom is taken as x- + il 'see' + -om, 'had been seen'; the form is inferred. The manuscript has xilo macut, divided as Brasseur divides it (x-ilom akut), and acut is taken as the particle, a form of cut 'then'; as that is not certain, the toggle respells its letters. rechabal 'his feeding place': r- 'his' + echa 'food' + -bal, the ending of place. Brasseur's French takes the line otherwise, the macaw climbing 'to see the husks of the fruit eaten by Hunahpu and Xbalanque'; the reading here is inferred.

sentences.t: Qui cacalen chi cut chuxe che ri Vucub Caquix; e maꜩamoh vlo ri caib ꜭaholab pa xac che.
sentences.l: Their lying-in-wait(?) in-turn then at-foot-of tree the Seven Macaw; they hidden(?) hither the two boys in leaves tree.
sentences.i: So they lay in wait for Vucub Caquix at the foot of the tree; the two boys were hidden among the leaves of the tree.
sentences.n: Qui cacalen 'their lying in wait' is inferred from Brasseur's French ('watching for Vucub Caquix at the foot of the tree'); he prints qakalem, and Ximénez writes plain c. chi cut, chic 'in turn' again. chuxe che 'at the foot of the tree': chu- (chi + v- 'its') + xe 'root, foot', the xe of the first line. e maꜩamoh 'they (were) hiding': e 'they' + maꜩamoh, not otherwise known (Brasseur 'came to hide'); inferred. vlo, a short form of vloc 'hither'. pa xac che 'among the leaves of the tree': xac 'leaf' (Brasseur xak, his k = q; the toggle shows xaq), not the xac 'blackened' of the last part.

sentences.t: Ta xopon cut Vucub Caquix, tacal chui recha ri tapal.
sentences.l: Then arrived then Seven Macaw, alighted(?) on-top-of his-food the tapal.
sentences.i: Then Vucub Caquix arrived and alighted on his food, the nance.
sentences.n: xopon 'he arrived (there)': x- + opon, the verb of copon in the last part. After xopon cut Ximénez wrote caib ꜭaholab 'two boys' and struck it through; it is left out. tacal comes three times in these lines and is taken as 'set, come to rest': here 'alighted', then the pellet 'struck', then the macaw 'landed'. All three are inferred from the setting (here Brasseur has 'to throw himself on the nances'). chui 'on top of', as above.

sentences.t: Cate cut ta xubaxic cumal ri Hunhunahpu; tacal vbac vvb chu caꜫate;
sentences.l: Then then when he-was-blowgunned by-them the Hunhunahpu; struck(?) its-bone his-blowgun at his-jaw(?);
sentences.i: Then he was shot with the blowgun by Hunhunahpu: the pellet of the blowgun struck him in the jaw;
sentences.n: xubaxic 'he was shot with the blowgun': x- + vb + -ax- (passive) + -ic. Here Ximénez writes Hunhunahpu, and he does so five times more (twice in the next paragraph, then in the next two and once when the boys take counsel), though the boy is Hunahpu at the start of this part, in the feeding-place line above (Hunahpu, Xbalanque) and at the end of the macaw's speech (vꜫab ri Hunahpu). Elsewhere in the book Hunhunahpu is the name of Hunahpu's father, and Brasseur notes the confusion. The name is printed as written, and l and i keep it. cumal 'by them' is the plural, though one name follows. vbac vvb 'the bone of his blowgun', that is, the clay pellet. chu caꜫate 'in his jaw' (chu, chi + v- 'his'): caꜫate is written with the tresillo (Brasseur cacate), and 'jaw, cheek' is inferred from his French ('in the cheek'). The word comes again as vcaꜫate and nu ꜫaꜫate.

sentences.t: chu racuh vchi ta xpe chui che, tacal chuvach vleu.
sentences.l: he-scraped(?) his-mouth when came on-top-of tree, landed(?) on-face-of earth.
sentences.i: he cried out as he came down from the top of the tree, and landed on the ground.
sentences.n: chu racuh vchi 'he cried out' is inferred. Brasseur's French has 'he let out great cries', and in a note further on he gives the same words (cu rakuh cu u chi) as 'he cried out', word for word 'he scraped his mouth'. Ximénez writes plain c in racuh. vchi 'his mouth' (chi 'mouth'). ta xpe chui che 'when he came from the top of the tree': xpe 'he came'. tacal chuvach vleu 'he landed on the face of the earth'.

sentences.t: Chi malmat cut ri Hunhunahpu, anim xbec; quiꜩih vi xbe vꜭhapa.
sentences.l: Hastily(?) then the Hunhunahpu, quickly he-went; truly there he-went his-seizing.
sentences.i: Then Hunhunahpu hurried; he went quickly; he went in earnest to seize him.
sentences.n: Chi malmat: the manuscript has chimalmat, the same letters as the name of the macaw's wife. It is divided as Brasseur divides it and taken as 'in haste' (his note: chimalmat in K'iche' means 'with eagerness'). The reading is doubtful. anim 'quickly'. xbec, xbe 'he went': x- + be 'go', with and without -c. quiꜩih 'truly'. vꜭhapa 'his seizing': v- 'his' + ꜭhap 'seize, grab' + -a, the act as a possessed noun after a verb of going, as vban after xrah above. The image has gh, that is ꜭh, where Brasseur prints chapa (Brasseur's ch does not tell ch from ch': he prints x-cha for xꜭha). The modern verb 'seize' is usually written chap, with plain ch, but the toggle follows the manuscript's letter, as with ꜭhaquix in the last part, and shows uch'apa.

sentences.t: Cate cut ta xcupix vlo vꜫab ri Hunhunahpu rumal ri Vucub Caquix; huzuc xꜩac vloc, xmeho vloc ꜩam vteleb.
sentences.l: Then then when was-seized(?) hither his-arm the Hunhunahpu by the Seven Macaw; suddenly fell hither, was-bent(?) hither tip his-shoulder.
sentences.i: But then Hunhunahpu's arm was caught by Vucub Caquix: at once it came away; it was bent back at the tip of the shoulder.
sentences.n: xcupix 'was caught': x- + cup + -ix (passive), inferred (Brasseur 'let himself be seized by an arm'). vꜫab 'his arm': ꜫab is both hand and arm (the tresillo, Brasseur gab). huzuc 'suddenly'. xꜩac vloc 'it fell, came away': ꜩac 'fall', as que ꜩac vloc in the last part. xmeho vloc 'it was bent back': meh 'bend' with -o, inferred; no prefix for 'he' is written. ꜩam vteleb 'the tip of his shoulder': ꜩam 'nose, tip' (the macaw's beak in the last part) and vteleb 'his shoulder' (Brasseur 'from the end of the shoulder'). The arm is torn off at the shoulder.

sentences.t: Ta xuꜩocopih chi cut Hunhunahpu ri Vucub Caquix; xavi vꜩ xquibano, ma nabe qui chacatahic tah rumal Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: Then he-let-go in-turn then Hunhunahpu the Seven Macaw; just good they-did, not first their being-brought-low (tah) by Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: Then Hunhunahpu let go of Vucub Caquix. They had done well: Vucub Caquix had not brought them low first.
sentences.n: xuꜩocopih 'he let go (of him)': x- + v- 'he' + ꜩocopih 'release'. The two names stand side by side, with nothing to mark which one let go; Brasseur makes it Hunhunahpu, and so does i. Here too the manuscript has Hunhunahpu. xavi vꜩ xquibano 'they did well' (vꜩ 'good'). ma ... tah 'not', around ma nabe qui chacatahic 'first their being brought low'. The sense is inferred: the boys lost an arm, but the macaw did not defeat them first (Brasseur 'without being able to be defeated first by Vucub Caquix').

sentences.t: Vcaam chi cut vꜫab ri Hunhunahpu rumal ri Vucub Caquix, ta xbe chi rochoch; xa chi ꜫu vlo tem vcaꜫate xoponic.
sentences.l: His-carrying(?) in-turn then his-arm the Hunhunahpu by the Seven Macaw, when he-went to his-home; only (chi ꜫu?) hither holding(?) his-jaw he-arrived.
sentences.i: Vucub Caquix carried off Hunhunahpu's arm and went to his home; he arrived there holding his jaw.
sentences.n: Vcaam 'carried by him' is taken as v- + cam 'take, carry', the verb of xquicam above, with the vowel written double (Brasseur 'carrying the arm of Hunhunahpu'); the form is inferred, and the toggle shows k'am. After vꜫab ri a small k is written above the line in a lighter hand; it is not printed. rochoch 'his home': r- + ochoch. xa chi ꜫu vlo tem vcaꜫate is a doubtful reading: the letter after chi is a tresillo, and the vowel after it is a or u (Brasseur cu); vcaꜫate may also be read vcoꜫate. tem is not otherwise known, and 'holding his jaw' follows Brasseur's French; it is inferred. xoponic 'he arrived': x- + opon + -ic.

sentences.t: “Naquipa mi xcamou chi la?” xꜭha cu ri Chimalmat, rixoquil Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: “What just-now took(?) to you(sir)?” said then the Chimalmat, his-wife Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: “What has happened to you, my lord?” said Chimalmat, the wife of Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: Naquipa 'what', as in the last part. mi 'just now'. la is taken as the respectful 'you': Brasseur's note gives chi la 'to Your Lordship', la being a word of reverence; the wife speaks to her husband as to a lord. xcamou is not clear. Brasseur prints qamou, that is ꜭ, perhaps the cam 'take' of xquicam with an ending -ou ('what has taken you?'); Ximénez writes plain c, and the toggle respells the letters. 'what has happened to you' is inferred.

sentences.t: “Naquipa ri? Ri e caib ꜭaxtoꜭ mi xi quivubah, mi xzilibatah nu ꜫaꜫate rumal.
sentences.l: “What (is) it? The they two demons just-now me they-blowgunned, just-now was-shaken-loose my jaw by-it.
sentences.i: “What could it be? Those two demons have shot me with the blowgun, and my jaw has been shaken loose by it.
sentences.n: ꜭaxtoꜭ 'demon, deceiver' (modern k'axtok'), the colonial word for the devil, used here by the macaw of the boys. Both its letters are g-shaped and read ꜭ (Brasseur qaxtok). xi quivubah 'they shot me with the blowgun' is taken as x- + i(n) 'me', with the n not written (as quiꜭohe 'I am' in the last part), + qui- 'they' + vubah 'shoot with the blowgun', as in the boys' plan. xzilibatah 'it was shaken loose': x- + zilib 'shake, move' (compare zilab above) + -atah; inferred. nu ꜫaꜫate 'my jaw', here with the tresillo twice (caꜫate above; Brasseur cacate). rumal 'by it', the shot. Brasseur takes rumal with the next line ('because of this ...'); here it ends this sentence.

sentences.t: Xa ca chuiu ahe ve, ca coxou chic.
sentences.l: Only they-are loose(?) gums(?) teeth, they-are aching(?) now.
sentences.i: My gums and my teeth are loose, and they ache now.
sentences.n: A hard line, taken from Brasseur's French ('my gums and my teeth are loosened, and they make me suffer much'). ca marks the ongoing state, twice. chuiu is taken as 'loose', ahe as 'gums', ve as 'teeth' (as in nay pu ve raxcavacoh in the macaw's boast in the last part), and coxou as 'ache'. All four are inferred, and the toggle respells their letters.

sentences.t: Mi nabe mi xnucam vloc chuvi ꜫaꜫ cut, chi xeque vi chi ꜩaiaba chuvi ꜫaꜫ, ta cul qui cama chic quiꜩih chic ꜭaxtoꜭ,” xꜭha ri Vucub Caquix, ta xuxequeba vꜫab ri Hunahpu.
sentences.l: Just-now first just-now I-brought hither on-top-of fire then, that hang there, that dangle(?) on-top-of fire, when comes their taking(?) again truly again demons,” said the Seven Macaw, when he-hung-up his-arm the Hunahpu.
sentences.i: But first I have just brought it here over the fire, so that it may hang there, may dangle over the fire, until they truly come to take it back, those demons,” said Vucub Caquix, as he hung up Hunahpu's arm.
sentences.n: xnucam 'I brought (it)': x- + nu- 'I' (the prefix of 'my' serving as the subject of a transitive verb) + cam 'take, bring', the verb of xquicam above (Brasseur qam, his q = ꜭ; the toggle shows k'am). What he brought is named only at the end: the arm. ꜫaꜫ 'fire' is written with the tresillo twice (Brasseur gag). At the first chuvi ꜫaꜫ 'over the fire' the words are underlined twice in darker ink, with a bracketed note in the margin, struck through, reading u cab ri hunhunahpu 'the arm of Hunhunahpu': a later reader's gloss, not printed. chi xeque vi, chi ꜩaiaba 'that it hang, that it dangle', a couplet: xeque 'hang' is the verb of xuxequeba below; ꜩaiaba is inferred (Brasseur tzayaba, 'suspended'), and the manuscript divides it chi ꜩa-|iaba across a line. ta cul qui cama 'until their taking comes': cul 'it comes' (c- + vl 'come, arrive here'), and qui cama 'their taking', perhaps again from cam 'take' (Brasseur gama, his g = ꜫ); Ximénez writes plain c, and the toggle respells the letters. xuxequeba 'he hung it up': x- + v- 'he' + xequeba. Here the manuscript has vꜫab ri Hunahpu, not Hunhunahpu.

sentences.t: Qui naohinic chic ri Hunhunahpu, Xbalanque; ta xquibih cut chirech hun mama, quiꜩih zac chic rizmal vi chi mama,
sentences.l: Their thinking again the Hunhunahpu, Xbalanque; then they-said then to-him one old-man, truly white now his-hair there of old-man,
sentences.i: Hunhunahpu and Xbalanque took thought again; then they spoke to an old man, an old man whose hair was truly white now,
sentences.n: Qui naohinic 'their pondering' (naoh 'mind' + -in + -ic): they took counsel. Here too Ximénez writes Hunhunahpu. xquibih 'they said, they spoke': x- + qui- 'they' + bih 'say' (the byih of xchicabyih). The letter after qui may be h (xquihih); b is printed, with Brasseur (qui-bih). chirech 'to him'. mama 'old man, grandfather'. rizmal 'his hair': r- 'his' + izmal 'hair' (Brasseur 'the hair of this old man'). chi mama 'of the old man'.

sentences.t: hun cu atit, quiꜩih quemel atit chic, xa que lucuquila chic chi rihtac vinac.
sentences.l: one then old-woman, truly bent(?) old-woman now, only they stooped(?) now in old(?) person.
sentences.i: and an old woman, an old woman truly bent over now; they were stooped now, as the old are.
sentences.n: hun cu atit 'and one old woman': the manuscript has hunca or huncu, Brasseur hun atit; cu, the particle, is printed. atit 'grandmother, old woman', as in Ratit Ꜫih; here and in every atit of this part the ß-ligature is read ti. quemel and lucuquila are not otherwise known: 'bent' and 'stooped' follow Brasseur's French ('all bent and doubled over by old age') and are inferred. que 'they' (c- + e): both of the old people. chi rihtac vinac: the manuscript has chirihtac, divided as chi + rihtac (Brasseur chi rihitak); rihtac is taken as 'old', with tac, the plural, 'as old people'; inferred.

sentences.t: Zaqui Nimac vbi mama; Zaqui Nima Ꜩiz cut vbi atit.
sentences.l: White Great(-ones?) his-name old-man; White Great Coati then her-name old-woman.
sentences.i: Zaqui Nimac was the old man's name; Zaqui Nima Tziz was the old woman's name.
sentences.n: The two names are the one name of the creators' litany in the first part, Zaqui Nimac Ꜯyꜩ 'White Great Coati', now shared between the two: zaqui 'white', nimac 'great' (with the plural -ac), nima 'great', ꜩiz 'coati'. Brasseur divides the man's name Zaki-Nim-Ak, nim ac 'great peccary', and Ximénez writes plain c in Nimac; the woman's he prints Zaki-Nima-Tzyiz. The manuscript runs zaquinimaꜩiz together, with the tz ligature ꜩ where the first part has ꜯ; the toggle shows Tz'iis, as in the first and third parts. Both names are kept in English.

sentences.t: Xeꜭha cu ri ꜭaholab chique ri atit, mama: “Quix cachbilah tah chi be ta cama ca ꜫab ruꜭ Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: They-said then the boys to-them the old-woman, old-man: “You we-accompany (tah) that go then take(?) our arm with Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: Then the boys said to the old woman and the old man: “Let us go along with you, to go and take back our arm from Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: Quix cachbilah tah: quix is c-, the ongoing prefix, + ix 'you (pl.)', the absolutive, here the object, the ones accompanied; c-, the form of ca- 'we' before a vowel, is the ergative subject, the ones who go along, + achbilah 'accompany' (Brasseur's note renders the words 'que vous nous accompagnions', word for word 'that you we accompany'), with tah, the particle of wishing: 'may we go with you'. The boys will walk with the old couple, as the next line says; Brasseur's French turns it round ('please go with us'). chi be 'that (we) go'. ta cama ca ꜫab 'to take our arm': cama as in qui cama above, inferred; ꜫab with the tresillo, as in every vꜫab of this part. 'our arm' is Hunahpu's: the boys speak as one. ruꜭ Vucub Caquix 'with Vucub Caquix, from him': ruꜭ, r- + uꜭ 'company'; the g-shaped letter is read ꜭ (Brasseur ruq).

sentences.t: Xa coh tere chivih.
sentences.l: Only we follow behind-you.
sentences.i: We will only follow behind you.
sentences.n: coh 'we (ongoing)': c- + oh. tere 'follow' (Brasseur 'we shall go behind you'). chivih 'behind you (pl.)': chi + iv- 'your' + ih 'back', the chivih of taking thought in the last part, here in its plain sense.

sentences.t: Qui ri ca mam ri cachbilan; caminac qui chuch, qui cahau;
sentences.l: They(?) the our grandsons whom we-accompany; dead their mother, their father;
sentences.i: ‘These are our grandsons, whom we take along with us; their mother, their father are dead;
sentences.n: Here begin the words the old couple are to say to Vucub Caquix, quoted inside the boys' speech; i sets them in inner quotation marks, and quix ꜭha 'you will say' closes them. Qui ri ca mam 'these are our grandsons': Qui is taken as 'they (are)' with Brasseur ('these are our grandsons'), and the form is not clear. mam is both grandfather and grandson (Brasseur's note), the old and the young ends of a line. cachbilan 'we accompany': c- 'we' (ca- before a vowel) + achbilan, the verb of the line above with another ending. caminac 'dead' (cam 'die' + -inac). qui chuch, qui cahau 'their mother, their father', the pair of ca nabe chuch, ca nabe cahau above.

sentences.t: quehe cut que tere cohila vi chiquih tala que ca zipah vi; rumal xa elezan vchicopil eiah ca ca bano, quix ꜭha.
sentences.l: thus then they follow cohila(?) there behind-us tala(?) they we-give(?) there; because only taking-out its-animals teeth we-do, you-will-say.
sentences.i: and so they follow along behind us, wherever we let them go; for all we do is draw the worms out of teeth,’ you will say.
sentences.n: que tere 'they follow' (c- + e 'they'). The rest of the clause, cohila vi chiquih tala que ca zipah vi, is not clear: chiquih is 'behind us' (chi + ca- 'our', written qu before a vowel, + ih 'back') and zipah 'give, grant', but cohila and tala are not otherwise known. 'wherever we let them go' follows Brasseur ('wherever it suits us to allow them') and is a guess. rumal xa ... ca ca bano 'for all we do is ...': ca (ongoing) + ca- 'we' + bano 'do'. elezan 'taking out' (elez 'take out', from el 'go out'). vchicopil 'its animals', the worms of the teeth; drawing them out was a healer's trade (Brasseur: 'the trade of pulling worms out of teeth'). eiah is taken as 'teeth' (e 'tooth', as ve above); inferred. quix ꜭha 'you will say': quix 'you (pl.)' + ꜭha 'say'; the manuscript writes quixgha as one word.

sentences.t: Quehe cu ri oh acalab chi rilo ri Vucub Caquix; xavi oh ꜭoh yauic i naoh,” xeꜭha ri e caib ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: Thus then the we children that he-see the Seven Macaw; just we there-are(?) giving your thought,” they-said the they two boys.
sentences.i: So Vucub Caquix will see us as children; and we shall be right there, giving you counsel,” said the two boys.
sentences.n: oh acalab 'we children': acalab, the plural of acal 'child' (Ximénez and Brasseur both write plain c; the toggle shows ak'alab', the modern word, with its ejective restored as certain). chi rilo 'that he see (us)': r- 'he' before a vowel + il 'see' + -o. xavi oh ꜭoh: ꜭoh is taken as ꜭo 'be there' + oh 'we', 'we shall be there' (Brasseur qoh; the g-shaped letter read ꜭ). yauic 'giving': ya 'give' + -ic, the verbal noun, with u (w) between. i naoh 'your mind, your counsel' (i- 'your (pl.)'): the boys will be at hand to prompt the old couple. The sense follows Brasseur ('to give you our counsel') and is inferred.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Good bala,” they-said then.
sentences.i: “Very well,” they said.
sentences.n: The old couple agree. vꜩ 'good'. bala, left unexplained in the third part (Brasseur 'at their ease'), is here 'very well' with vꜩ, as Brasseur has it ('C'est fort bien!'); its sense is inferred. The manuscript runs vꜩbala together at the foot of a page, and the last word, cut, stands at the top of the next. The old couple's visit to Vucub Caquix follows in the next part.
